title: QaiJi IR: An Eight-Layer Intermediate Representation Family for Hybrid Quantum-Classical Compilation
abstract: Hybrid quantum-classical compilers exchange programs among circuit, control-flow, pulse, device, and physical representations. Existing formats make different abstraction choices, so the properties that must survive a lowering step are often enforced by tool-specific code rather than stated in a common intermediate representation (IR). We present QaiJi IR, an eight-layer family organized by a \emph{five-axis semantic contract} for data, semantics, lowering, runtime, and verification. Its L4 SemanticIR records the operation class, declared equivalence level, optimization role, and classical-feedback model as attributes, and maps operation classes to ISA-neutral hardware actions.   The prototype provides typed quantum and classical circuit nodes, OpenQASM~2 compatibility input, canonical OpenQASM~3 output, explicit rejection of unsupported constructs, and executable gate-convention checks. A representative measurement-conditioned program reaches a canonical QASM fixed point, acquires a measurement-to-condition edge, passes an exact aggregate consistency check, and produces a symbolic pulse template. For a one-bit active-reset case, device lowering materializes ALU/FPROC records and a conditional branch. Running the resulting virtual pulse processing unit (VPPU) program with externally supplied outcomes 0 and 1 respectively skips and executes the conditional drive. These tests validate the represented compiler path and binary branch behavior. They do not establish a physical feedback loop, because the simulator cannot yet apply mid-circuit measurement collapse and continue the same dynamical trajectory.
summary: This paper presents QaiJi IR, a novel eight-layer intermediate representation designed to standardize the compilation process for hybrid quantum-classical algorithms. It enforces semantic correctness across multiple abstraction levels using a five-axis contract. The framework successfully validates the compilation path for measurement-based control flow, providing a structured tool for quantum compiler design.
main_problem: Existing hybrid quantum-classical compilers lack a common intermediate representation (IR) to enforce properties that must survive the lowering from high-level abstractions to physical hardware.
main_result: The authors introduce QaiJi IR, an eight-layer family governed by a five-axis semantic contract, which successfully models and tests the compilation path for measurement-conditioned quantum programs.
method: They propose QaiJi IR, which uses a five-axis semantic contract (Data, Semantics, Lowering, Runtime, Verification) and an L4 SemanticIR to map abstract operations to ISA-neutral hardware actions.
model_or_system: The model is the compilation pipeline for hybrid quantum-classical computation, involving quantum circuits, classical control flow, and pulse/device representations.
key_observables: The successful materialization of ALU/FPROC records and the execution of a conditional branch (skip/execute) on a virtual pulse processing unit (VPPU) for an active-reset case.
important_parameters: The five axes of the semantic contract; the eight-layer structure of the IR.
main_assumptions: The current simulator cannot apply mid-circuit measurement collapse and continue the full dynamical trajectory, limiting validation to consistency checks rather than full physical fidelity.
figures_summary: Figure 2 illustrates the eight-layer QaiJi IR structure with side connections for dynamics and traces; Figure 3 summarizes the six-stage lowering pipeline and its interface invariants.
paper_structure: The paper introduces the problem of compiler abstraction gaps, details the QaiJi IR structure (eight layers, five-axis contract), describes the six-stage lowering pipeline, and validates the framework using measurement-conditioned and active-reset examples.
why_interesting: It provides a rigorous, structured framework for managing the complex compilation stack required for near-term quantum hardware, which is crucial for any physicist working on implementing quantum algorithms on real devices.
